slots.title: Audi’s first U.S. plant lands in Georgia
slots.body:
Audi is planning its first U.S. assembly plant in Georgia.

The WSJ ties the move to stalled sales elsewhere and tariff pressure on imported autos.

It is a policy-and-trade story, not a single earnings print.

Which part matters more to you: jobs on the ground in Georgia, or how tariffs reshape where cars get built?

slots.title: Russian diesel tanker bound for New York
slots.body:
Fox Business says a Russian diesel tanker is en route to New York.

The cargo is about 40,000 tons.

The piece links the shipment to a Trump deal with Putin framed around easing fuel prices.

A retired general quoted in the story says that volume covers only a couple of hours of U.S. diesel demand.

Brent crude settled at 116.72, up 3.1% on the session in the injected cross-asset data.

Does a one-off cargo change how you read U.S.–Russia energy politics, or is scale the whole story?

slots.title: Ten names drive two-thirds of profit growth
slots.body:
The WSJ says ten companies account for roughly two-thirds of corporate profit growth.

Nvidia and Micron are among the names cited as AI-linked giants in that group.

That is a concentration statistic about profits, not a screen ranking.

The S&P 500 closed at 7,623.68, down 0.5% on the session.

The Nasdaq Composite closed at 25,955.34, down 0.2%.

When profit growth clusters that tightly, do you treat it as a macro risk or as a sector story?

slots.title: U.S. cash session — Oct. 24, 2026
slots.body:
The Dow Jones Industrial Average led the decline among major U.S. indexes, closing down 1.2% (652.82 points) at 52,215.16 after trading between 52,055.10 and 52,696.70.

The S&P 500 finished down 0.5% at 7,623.68, with an intraday band of 7,612.07 to 7,660.15 and reported volume of about 2.75 billion shares in the injected figure.

The Nasdaq Composite slipped 0.2% to 25,955.34; the Russell 2000 was down 0.3% at 2,775.90.

Oil was a standout on the cross-asset tape: Brent crude rose 3.1% to 116.72, and the United States Oil Fund ($USO) closed up 4.3% at 169.53 with a session high of 169.96 in the data.

Exxon ($XOM) and Chevron ($CVX) rose 2.8% and 2.9% to 183.21 and 233.21 respectively, each printing a day high that matched the injected 52-week high fields (183.75 for XOM, 233.74 for CVX).

Gold futures (GCUSD in the feed) fell 1.3% to 4,007.90, off as much as 52.50 from the prior close in the bundle.

The VIX, the market’s volatility gauge, rose 2.2% to 19.45 after touching 20.66 intraday.

Several large consumer and household names closed lower by about 2%: Coca-Cola ($KO) -2.8% to 92.71, Home Depot ($HD) -2.4% to 319.83, PepsiCo ($PEP) -2.2% to 135.77, and Procter & Gamble ($PG) -2.1% to 161.02.

Semiconductor-related megacaps split: AMD ($AMD) +1.7% to 516.79, Taiwan Semiconductor ($TSM) +1.5% to 418.51, and ASML ($ASML) +0.7% to 1,571.80, while NVIDIA ($NVDA) closed down 0.6% at 210.96 on heavy reported volume of about 79.7 million shares.

Alphabet ($GOOGL) lost 1.2% to 320.21, Meta ($META) -1.0% to 642.62, Netflix ($NFLX) -1.8% to 65.85, and Apple ($AAPL) was nearly flat at -0.1% to 347.73.

Among active names in the injected list, AT&T ($T) stood out at -8.0% to 20.93; Robert Half ($RHI) rose 21.7% to 45.87 in the liquid-gainers screen.

The injected economic and earnings calendars for this bundle were empty, so no new macro print or corporate actuals were listed for this close.

Treasury yields in the feed carried a 2026-10-22 stamp: the 10-year at 5.0% and the 2s10s spread at 0.31 percentage points in that snapshot.

Bitcoin (BTCUSD) was up 0.1% to 80,856.23; the dollar-proxy ETF $UUP ticked up 0.2% to 28.96, and EUR/USD was down 0.2% at 1.12 in the cross-asset block.

Overseas indexes in the same payload were mixed ahead of or outside U.S. hours: Hang Seng +0.7% to 23,093.40, while the Nikkei 225, FTSE 100, and Germany proxy (EWG) posted modest losses of 0.3% to 1.0% in the injected overseas section.

slots.title: Fed rate call lands Wednesday at 4%
slots.body:
Oct. 28, 6:00 p.m.
ET: U.S. Fed interest-rate decision.

Consensus estimate: 4% — same as the prior 4% setting.

Same day, 6:00 p.m.
ET: FOMC economic projections (growth, unemployment, and rate path the committee sketches for markets).

6:30 p.m.
ET: Fed press conference — officials explain the decision in plain terms after the statement drops.

That trio is the fixed calendar for the week; it sets the baseline for how borrowing costs are described until the next meeting.

Which part do you usually read first — the statement, the dot plot, or the Q&A?

slots.title: Q3 GDP and September PCE both Oct. 29
slots.body:
Oct. 29, 8:30 a.m.
ET — one batch of prints:

GDP growth rate (Q3, quarter-over-quarter): estimate 3.2%; prior quarter 2.2%.

That GDP figure is the broad “how fast the economy grew last quarter” number.

Same timestamp — personal spending (Sep, month-over-month): estimate 0.3%; prior 0.9%.

Personal income (Sep, month-over-month): estimate 0.3%; prior 0.2%.

Core PCE price index (Sep, month-over-month): estimate 0.3%; prior 0.2% — “core PCE” means inflation in consumer prices with food and energy stripped out, a gauge the Fed references often.

Core PCE (Sep, year-over-year): estimate 3.1%; prior 3.0%.

Also in the release: initial jobless claims (Oct. 24 week) estimate 196K vs. prior 194K — weekly count of new unemployment filings.

Everything above resolves Thursday morning; no single headline number tells the whole story.

Which line in that bundle do you treat as the main read — growth, spending, or core PCE?
